title: The deep lake (82–89)
hook: the wise grow calm like a deep, clear, still lake; few reach the other shore

segments.voice: Yesterday, pandita, the wise one, who treats correction like treasure and stands like a rock in blame and praise. Your line: the rock doesn't shake. Today, the end of the week, and the end of chapter six.

Toss a pebble into a shallow puddle. Mud clouds up everywhere, the whole thing churns, and it takes a long time to clear. Now picture a deep mountain lake early on a windless morning. You can see down through the water to stones far below, and the surface holds the whole sky: clouds, trees, the far ridge. Drop a pebble in, and the rings spread, and soften, and the lake is still again. Same pebble. Very different water.
screen: `A PEBBLE IN A PUDDLE.` → `A DEEP LAKE AT DAWN.` → `SAME PEBBLE, DIFFERENT WATER.`

segments.voice: Verse eighty-two, in Müller's English: “Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake.” Three qualities. Deep: things reach far down without stirring up mud. Smooth: the surface isn't whipped around by every gust. Still: it reflects what's there, instead of distorting it. Verse eighty-three says good people walk on, whatever happens: not lifted up by pleasure or thrown down by pain. It's yesterday's rock, turned to water. Then verses eighty-five and eighty-six bring in a picture that will come back on this path: the other shore. “Few are there among men who arrive at the other shore (become Arhats); the other people here run up and down the shore.” Picture a riverbank crowded with busy people, running this way and that along the edge. Very few actually cross. The other shore is freedom, nibbana; this side is the round of wanting and worrying. Verse eighty-six says those who live by the teaching will cross over. And the chapter closes with the wise leaving the dark, following the bright, and shining in this world. Look back over the week: the bee, the lotus on the heap, long is the night, the spoon and the soup, milk that turns slowly, the rock that doesn't shake, and now still water. The week ends on the simplest of its pictures: water, left alone long enough to settle.
screen: `DEEP, SMOOTH AND STILL.` · `NOT LIFTED, NOT THROWN DOWN.` · `RUNNING UP AND DOWN THE SHORE.` · `THE WEEK, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `STILL WATER.`

segments.voice: Let the body settle like a lake in its bed, and let the breath slow on its own. Thoughts will drop in like pebbles; don't grab them or chase the ripples, just watch the rings spread, soften and fade. The lake doesn't have to do anything to go still again; it only has to stop stirring.
The deep lake. The wise grow serene like deep, smooth, still water, and few cross to the other shore.
Your line: still water. Deep, smooth and still, it settles on its own. A whole week, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the image of a still, clear lake for a settled mind in meditation, and the other shore appears as an image for nibbana in chants and teachings.

original.note: Pali: a lake, from verse eighty-two: 'yathapi rahado gambhiro,' like a deep lake.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm person is someone nothing reaches.
what it means: things reach the wise deeply, but don't churn up mud; the surface settles and reflects clearly.
what a scholar hears: 'rahado gambhiro vippasanno anavilo': deep, very clear, unstirred; 'paragu,' one gone to the far shore, is a standing epithet of the awakened.
recall: one who chooses the right flower
